# Finnish Immigration Service

August 22, 2024

 

Hey everyone! I have a quick question regarding EU registration at Finnish Immigration Service. Is it true that I can book an appointment in any of their offices to register my right of residence? 

The reason I am asking is that I live in Espoo, and the soonest time to attend the office in Helsinki is in the mid-November. That’s why I started considering attending the office in Lahti, where the soonest possible appointment is in the beginning of September. However, when booking an appointment on Migri.fi, I noticed the following note (attached screenshot). 

Is this note is made just to specify that the only office in Helsinki is IHH or that I cannot register my right of residence in other offices?

Thanks in advance!

# International House Helsinki Relocates to Pasila ‘Suomi-piste’ Service Hub

 Jun 2, 2026

 Finn Visas & Immigration Team @ VisaHQ

 Helsinki’s one-stop service centre for newcomers, International House Helsinki (IHH), opened its doors this morning at a new address—Ratapihantie 7 in the rapidly developing Pasila business district. The relocation, effective 1 June 2026, brings IHH under the roof of the government’s brand-new Suomi-piste (“Finland-Point”) customer-service concept, which gathers multiple public bodies in a single accessible building next to Pasila rail station. IHH is best known among expatriates and global mobility teams for handling EU-citizen registration appointments, issuing Finnish personal identity codes, and providing multilingual advice on taxation, social security and local employment rules. All these services continue unchanged, but visitors now benefit from extended opening hours (09:00–16:00 Monday-Wednesday and Friday; 10:30–16:00 Thursday), barrier-free access and direct rail links to Helsinki Airport and city-centre hotels. According to the Finnish Immigration Service, the move is part of a broader digital-first overhaul of customer service. The Suomi-piste model co-locates Migri desk officers with staff from the Tax Administration, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) and the Social Insurance Institution (Kela). New arrivals can therefore register their right of residence, obtain a tax card, apply for a social-security number and receive orientation counselling in a single visit. For employers, the consolidation promises faster onboarding of foreign hires. Whereas previously an assignee might have needed three separate appointments across town, HR teams can now book one time slot through Migri’s online system and track progress via Enter Finland. Early feedback from pilot users indicates that average time-to-ID-number issuance has dropped from ten days to three. Companies should update welcome packs, relocation guides and map links immediately. The old IHH premises on Lintulahdenkuja will close permanently and no longer accept walk-in visitors. Those with appointments booked before 1 June have been automatically re-scheduled to the Pasila site, and confirmation messages have been sent to the email address on file. 

 Source: Finnish Immigration Service – Service Point Directory

Moving to Helsinki (2026): The Complete Relocation Guide - Flyto

## Moving to Helsinki (2026): The Complete Relocation Guide

Author: Flyto Editorial Team · Reviewed by: Ariel Keisa, Founder & CEO in

Last reviewed: 7.9.2026

Helsinki is Finland’s capital and by far its largest city — around 675,000 people in the city itself and roughly 1.6 million across the greater Helsinki region — and it is the country’s main landing point for international arrivals. It is also a genuinely Nordic city to move into: much of the desirable housing sits in early-1900s Jugend blocks and 1950s walk-ups with no lift and tight stairwells, the classic city block wraps around an inner courtyard, your moving truck cannot simply reserve the kerb outside the door, and for a large part of the year the loading itself happens on snow and ice in the dark. This guide covers the practical mechanics of moving to Helsinki in 2026 — the truck-and-building logistics only a mover knows, where to live and what rent really costs, how to find a flat and register at DVV, and what monthly life actually costs — with official sources throughout.

Freshness note: prices and rules verified against hel.fi, suomi.fi, dvv.fi, International House Helsinki, HSL, Tilastokeskus, the Finnish Meteorological Institute and Helsinki city statistics in 2026. Fees and rents move — confirm figures with the linked authorities before you rely on them.

## Quick answer: moving to Helsinki in 2026

What does it cost to move to Helsinki? An international household move (a full flat) typically lands in the low-to-mid four figures from within Europe and higher from overseas, driven mostly by volume, distance and access. Because Helsinki’s access difficulties — no-lift Jugend buildings, courtyards, winter conditions — add real cost, get a fixed quote for your specific address rather than a generic estimate: get a Flyto quote here.

How long does the move take? Road moves from within the EU are usually a few days to about two weeks door-to-door; overseas sea freight runs several weeks. The two Helsinki-specific quirks everyone underestimates: nearly half of the city’s apartment buildings have no lift (Helsinki city statistics), so a bulky sofa often has to go in through a window on an external furniture lift (muuttonostin); and there is no free ”book a spot” for the truck — for a disruptive move you take out a paid permit to use the public area (City of Helsinki area-use permit).

## Key takeaways

- Nearly half of Helsinki’s apartment buildings have no lift. At the end of 2018 about 46% of the city’s apartment buildings — roughly 4,900 buildings holding some 90,000 flats — had no elevator, most of them older or mid-century walk-ups (Helsinki city statistics). This is exactly why an external furniture lift (muuttonostin / ulkohissi) is so often needed.
- Your moving truck cannot just reserve the kerb. You may briefly stop to load bulky items, but for a genuinely disruptive move you need a paid permit to take a street or public area into temporary use, granted by the Urban Environment Division (suomi.fi; application via hel.fi).
- Winter is a real operational factor. Permanent snow cover in the capital region normally sets in only after Christmas and clears on average around the turn of March–April (Finnish Meteorological Institute) — snow, ice and short, dark days make winter loading slower and worth planning carefully.
- Register at DVV to get your kotikunta and henkilötunnus. Newcomers register in the Population Information System at DVV — in Helsinki mainly by appointment at International House Helsinki — where you also apply for a personal identity code (henkilötunnus) and municipality of residence (kotikunta), which unlocks public healthcare, daycare and much else (International House Helsinki).
- Deposit is capped and usually 1–2 months. A rental deposit (vuokravakuus) is legally limited to at most three months’ rent (Act on Residential Leases, §8), and in practice landlords typically ask for one to two months (Vuokralaiset ry).

## 1. The move into Helsinki — logistics only a mover knows

This is the part generic ”moving to Helsinki” guides skip, and it is exactly where a move goes wrong. Helsinki’s inner districts were built for courtyards and trams, not for a full-size removal truck, and half the year the weather is against you. Four things determine whether your move day runs smoothly.

### Parking the truck: the loading exception and the area-use permit

Helsinki does not offer a simple online ”book a moving-van bay” service, and you cannot count on a free stretch of kerb outside the building. There are two legal routes:

- The brief loading exception. A vehicle may stop even on a footway or cycle path for the short time it takes to load or unload, but only when there is a compelling reason, the load is genuinely bulky (furniture, white goods, a piano — not hand-carried boxes), at least one metre is left clear for pedestrians, and the driver stays with the vehicle ready to move it (City of Helsinki, ”Sujuvaa pysäköintiä”). This covers a quick, simple move — it does not reserve you a space.
- The area-use permit. For a demanding move that will block a traffic lane or occupy a parking space for longer, you apply for a permit to take a public area into temporary use (lupa yleisen alueen käyttöön) from the Urban Environment Division. The service is paid, the same office that handles street works and events grants it, and you can arrange temporary no-parking signs to keep the space clear (suomi.fi; application form and contact hel.fi, luvat@hel.fi).

Knowing which route your address needs — and arranging the permit and signs in advance when it does — is the difference between a truck parked at the door and one stranded a block away.

### Winter: snow, ice, darkness and frozen loading

This is the genuinely Nordic factor. In the Helsinki region, permanent snow cover typically arrives only after Christmas and disappears on average around the turn of March and April (Finnish Meteorological Institute), but sub-zero spells, ice and slush can bracket that window from November into April. A winter move means snow and ice on the access routes and courtyard, ramps and pavements that need clearing and gritting before anything heavy is carried, daylight that in December runs to only about six hours, and cold that makes long carries and lift set-up slower. None of this stops a move — Finns move house all winter — but it has to be planned for: earlier start times, clearing and salting the path, protecting floors from meltwater and grit, and allowing more time. A mover who works Helsinki winters builds this in; a generic van hire discovers it at 8 a.m. on a frozen loading bay.

### Jugend blocks, 1950s walk-ups and the muuttonostin

Much of the housing people actually want in Helsinki sits in early-1900s Jugend (Art Nouveau) blocks in Kruununhaka, Ullanlinna, Eira, Punavuori and Katajanokka, or in the 1950s rintamamiestalo-era walk-ups further out. Many of these buildings have no lift, and where a lift exists it is often a small original cage that will not take a wardrobe. Citywide, roughly 46% of apartment buildings had no elevator at the end of 2018 — about 4,900 buildings and 90,000 flats (Helsinki city statistics).

The practical consequence: sofas, wardrobes, double beds and appliances frequently will not fit up a narrow, turning Helsinki stairwell. The standard solution is an external furniture lift (muuttonostin / ulkohissi) — a ladder hoist run up the facade to bring bulky items in through a window or balcony, reaching the upper floors and attic conversions. It needs its own space at the kerb, which is another reason the parking arrangement matters. A good mover measures the stairwell, the floor and the doorways before the day and books the lift in advance, rather than discovering the problem when the sofa is wedged on the second-floor landing.

### Courtyards, gate arches and one-way streets

The classic Helsinki block is built around an inner courtyard (sisäpiha), reached through a gate arch (porttikäytävä) that is usually too low and too narrow for a truck to enter. A flat in the courtyard wing (piharakennus) can mean carrying every box a long way from the street, across the yard, and the yard itself is often reserved for residents’ parking and bins. Add the peninsula’s one-way streets, tram tracks and cycle lanes, and ”just park outside” is rarely simple. None of this is a problem if it is planned for — and all of it is a bad surprise if it is not.

## 2. Where to live — Helsinki neighborhoods by profile

Helsinki’s character changes district by district, and the water is never far. The figures below are indicative average asking rents (€/m²/month) for late 2025 from Asunnollehinta.fi, cross-checked against Tilastokeskus rent statistics (Statistics Finland) and Helsinki’s own market review (kaupunkitieto.hel.fi). The citywide average sits around €20/m²; smaller flats cost far more per square metre than large ones, so a studio in a ”cheap” area can still be dear.

Central and characterful:

- Kamppi / Kluuvi — the centre (~€23/m²) — maximum convenience: the main station, metro, trams, shops and offices at the door. You pay the top rents and get little neighbourhood calm; some blocks empty out after work.
- Kruununhaka (~€18/m²) — the dignified old town beside the harbour and university: Jugend and Empire buildings, quiet cobbled streets, older residents and academics. Beautiful and central, mostly no-lift stairwells, and short on nightlife.
- Punavuori (~€21/m²) — the design district: independent shops, cafés and bars in handsome early-1900s blocks. Young professionals and creatives; lively, walkable and pricey, with the usual weekend noise near the bar streets.
- Eira & Ullanlinna (~€17–22/m²) — the seaside establishment: villas, embassies and grand Jugend flats by the shore parks. Prestigious and calm; the per-m² average is pulled down by large family apartments, but small flats are expensive and rare.

Best for young professionals and nightlife:

- Kallio (~€21/m²) — the classic first Helsinki address: small flats, cheap eats and the densest bar scene in the city, historically working-class and now thoroughly mixed. Central and full of life, but noisy and short on space.
- Sörnäinen (~€21/m²) — Kallio’s edgier neighbour by the metro, with the Kalasatama towers and new-build rising nearby; convenient and buzzy, uneven street to street.
- Töölö (~€19–20/m²) — elegant and central, wrapping the bay and the big parks, opera and concert hall: refined 1920s–30s blocks, popular with professionals and families alike. Calmer and greener than Kallio, and priced for it.

Quieter, greener, good value:

- Vallila (~€18/m²) — brick 1920s blocks and a famous wooden-house enclave (Puu-Vallila); down-to-earth, well connected by tram, gentrifying steadily. Good value close to the centre.
- Kumpula & Käpylä (~€17–18/m²) — leafy, low-rise and family-friendly, with garden-city wooden houses and the university campus; calm and green, a little further out, below the city average for larger flats.
- Lauttasaari (~€19/m²) — the popular island suburb one metro stop west: sea on every side, 1950s–60s blocks and newer builds, beaches and quick access to the centre. A favourite of families and remote workers.

Neighbouring cities (same commuter region):

- Espoo — Tapiola (~€19–27/m²) — the western neighbour: green, spacious and family-oriented, home to Aalto University and much of the tech sector. Tapiola is a leafy garden city on the metro; Espoo’s citywide average is close to Helsinki’s (~€20/m²), with Pohjois-Tapiola among the priciest spots (~€27/m²).
- Vantaa (generally below Helsinki, top areas rarely above ~€25/m²) — the northern neighbour around the airport, well linked by the Ring Rail Line; more space for the money, plainer in places, a sensible pick if budget or commute to the airport matters.

## 3. The Helsinki housing market — how flats are actua
